set.hook: A Raval dairy-bar since 1870, where the Viaders invented Cacaolat; now in the fifth generation's hands.
set.why: Rafaela Coma opened a dairy here in 1870 and the Viaders took it over around 1904. In 1931 Joan Viader Roger tasted a cold chocolate milk at the Budapest fair and patented his own at home that December: Cacaolat, a brand the family sold long ago. On 7 May 2026 Marc Espuny Casademunt became owner, a month before his mother, Mercè Casademunt Viader, retired at 67, ending fears the granja would close with her.

set.hook: A Gothic Quarter shop selling sweets made in Spanish convents, with a café in the vaults below.
set.why: Caelum buys from enclosed religious houses across Spain and sells what the nuns and monks make: truffles from the sisters of Valladolid, cider cake from Santa Inés in Seville, tea biscuits from the Convento Madre de Dios in Cáceres, and Trappist beers. The café is downstairs, under vaulted stone in what is described as the remains of medieval baths; whether they were public baths or a Jewish women's mikveh is still argued.

set.hook: Escribà's pastry counter inside the 1902 mosaic shopfront of the Antiga Casa Figueras on La Rambla.
set.why: Antoni Ros i Güell redesigned this Rambla shopfront in 1902 with mosaics, stained glass and stucco for the Figueras pasta business; the Escribà pastry family took it over in 1986. The Rambla works hurt it: Christian Escribà closed for about five months in 2025, cut five of seven staff, reopened on 3 December 2025 behind a shutter repainted by two Sitges artists, and expected to shut again from 15 January 2026 for the pavement phase.

set.hook: A standing-room cava bar by Port Vell, pouring its own pink cava since 1969.
set.why: Since 1969 this narrow room off Port Vell has sold its own cava, made under the Berenguer Ramon label, at the counter and by the bottle in the shop. The house rosat semi-sec is also sold by Barcelona wine retailers, so the bar doubles as the cellar door for its own wine.

set.hook: A 1970 white-banquette tortilla room under life-size photo silhouettes of Karin Leiz.
set.why: Photographer Leopoldo Pomés opened Flash Flash in 1970 with architect Alfonso Milà, who designed the white leather room with Federico Correa. The black-and-white figures on the walls are cut from Pomés's photographs of the model Karin Leiz, the same figure from his advertising work. The kitchen turns out more than fifty tortillas, and the room has changed so little that it reached its fiftieth birthday in 2020 still looking like 1970.
